title: Critical Evaluation of AI Output
description: Build the habit of evaluating AI responses critically — the most important skill for safe and effective AI use.

data.text: The most dangerous AI user is one who never questions the output. The most effective AI user has a fast, reliable habit for deciding when to trust, when to verify, and when to discard an AI response. This lesson builds that habit.

data.caption: Match your verification effort to the stakes — not every AI output needs the same level of scrutiny
data.definition:
graph TD
  T1["🟢 Brainstorming & creative ideas\nUse freely, no verification needed"]
  T2["🟡 First draft of internal document\nRead through, edit as needed"]
  T3["🟠 Client-facing or public content\nVerify claims, review tone carefully"]
  T4["🔴 Specific facts, stats, citations\nAlways check primary source"]
  T5["⛔ Medical, legal, financial decisions\nNever rely solely on AI"]

rows: ⛔ Do not rely on AI alone

data.text: Five questions to ask every AI response

items: Did it actually answer the question I asked? (AI often answers a related but slightly different question)
Are there any specific facts I should verify before acting on this? (dates, names, numbers, citations, URLs)
Is the reasoning internally consistent? (does the conclusion follow from the logic presented?)
Is this missing something my own knowledge tells me should be here?
Would a qualified person in this domain agree with this conclusion?

data.text: Red flags that always warrant verification

items: Any specific percentage, statistic, or data point
Author names, study names, or journal citations
Exact dates, especially for recent or historical events
URLs or links to external resources
Claims about current market prices, stock values, or live data
Any legal or medical statement you plan to rely on

data.title: Critical evaluation in practice
data.content:
You ask AI: "What percentage of people work remotely in the US?"

AI answers: "According to a 2023 McKinsey study, approximately 58% of American workers have the option to work remotely at least part of the time, with 35% working remotely full time."

🔍 Critical evaluation:
✅ This sounds plausible and McKinsey does publish this research
⚠️ But — did this specific study say exactly 58%? And 35% full time? Those numbers need checking.
📋 Action: Search "McKinsey remote work 2023" and verify the exact figures before quoting them.

This takes 60 seconds and protects your credibility.

data.text: Rule of thumb: the more consequential the downstream action, the more upstream verification you need. Calibrate verification effort to stakes, not paranoia.

data.title: Build this habit
points: Not every AI output needs verification — match effort to stakes
Specific facts (numbers, citations, names, dates) always need a second check
Your domain expertise is your best first filter for quality
Five questions: Did it answer? Verify facts? Consistent? Missing anything? Expert agreement?
Treat AI as a brilliant first draft — your judgment is still the final step

data.text: Critical review prompts that improve judgment
Critical evaluation improves when you ask the model to expose uncertainty, alternatives, and missing evidence. This shifts interaction from answer consumption to analytical review.

cards.title: Trust but verify
cards.description: Default to trusting AI output, then spot-check critical claims. Fast but can miss subtle errors.

cards.title: Healthy skepticism
cards.description: Assume output needs verification, especially for facts and numbers. Slightly slower but dramatically reduces error propagation.

cards.title: Red-team mindset
cards.description: Actively look for flaws, inconsistencies, and unsupported claims. Slowest but most thorough for high-stakes decisions.
